The target sample size was set before data collection on the basis of previous literature, for the critical test (H3; equalizing perceived speed between peripheral and foveal stimuli should reduce the difference in their perceived durations). This expected effect size was derived by reasoning from two independent literatures: Peripheral stimuli appear substantially slower than foveal stimuli moving at the same physical speed (Hassan et al., 2016; Johnston & Wright, 1986), and perceived duration increases approximately in proportion to log speed (Brown, 1995; Kaneko & Murakami, 2009). Because these literatures use different paradigms and dependent measures (speed matching and duration reproduction/production, respectively), the expected OR for a 2IFC duration comparison could not be read directly from prior work; OR = 0.90 represents a deliberately conservative estimate of the predicted shift, chosen so that the design would not be underpowered if the true effect were small. text.text: Visual processing varies systematically with eccentricity: Stimuli in the periphery are perceived as slower, lower in contrast, and shorter in duration compared with foveal stimuli.
Whether these asymmetries reflect a single underlying mechanism, such that removing one asymmetry eliminates others, or partly distinct mechanisms remains unknown.

We tested this question for perceived motion speed and duration, both underestimated in the periphery, by asking whether perceptually equalizing motion speed across the visual field eliminates or reduces the foveal duration bias.
In a two-phase design, each participant's peripheral speed bias was first measured at two eccentricities (approximately 11° and 22°).
Participants then compared the durations of foveal and peripheral random dot kinematograms (100-1,600 ms) under physical or perceptual speed equality.
The calibration showed robust peripheral speed underestimation at both eccentricities, increasing with distance from fixation.
Under physical speed equality, the foveal stimulus was judged to last longer than the peripheral one.

Critically, perceptual speed equalization reduced this foveal duration bias by approximately 60%, and this reduction was larger for participants whose calibrated speed correction was larger, consistent with a doseresponse relationship.
However, a significant residual bias persisted even after perceptual speed equalization.

These findings suggest that asymmetries between foveal and peripheral vision do not reflect a single underlying mechanism, but rather reflect a number of partly distinct yet related mechanisms that operate on different features, in this case motion speed and duration.

Visual processing varies systematically across the visual field: As stimuli move from the fovea toward the periphery, spatial resolution declines (Anstis, 1974) and contrast sensitivity decreases (Rovamo et al., 1978).
text.formatted: Visual processing varies systematically across the visual field: As stimuli move from the fovea toward the periphery, spatial resolution declines <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anstis, 1974)</ref> and contrast sensitivity decreases <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Rovamo et al., 1978)</ref>.

text.text: These eccentricity-dependent changes affect the perceived magnitude of many stimulus features, including size, numerosity, and speed (for a review, see Stewart et al., 2020), and such features in turn interact directionally with the perception of time (Brown, 1995; Cai & Connell, 2015; Eagleman, 2008; Eagleman & Pariyadath, 2009; Karsilar et al., 2025 Karsilar et al., , 2026;; Walsh, 2003; Xuan et al., 2007).

text.text: A key question is whether these various eccentricity-dependent asymmetries are manifestations of a single underlying mechanism, in which case removing the asymmetry in one dimension should eliminate it in another, or whether they arise from partly distinct processes.
The present study addresses this question for two particularly well-established asymmetries: those in perceived motion speed and perceived duration.
One of the most robust perceptual asymmetries across the visual field is the underestimation of motion speed in peripheral vision.

Peripheral stimuli moving at the same physical speed as foveal stimuli are perceived as slower (Brooks & Mather, 2000; Tynan & Sekuler, 1982), and the magnitude of this underestimation scales with eccentricity (Johnston & Wright, 1986).
text.formatted: Peripheral stimuli moving at the same physical speed as foveal stimuli are perceived as slower <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brooks & Mather, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Tynan & Sekuler, 1982)</ref>, and the magnitude of this underestimation scales with eccentricity <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Johnston & Wright, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: The effect is substantial: Under typical viewing conditions, peripheral gratings appear approximately 10% slower at 6° and 20% slower at 32° eccentricity even when their perceived contrast is matched to that of foveal gratings, and slow gratings appear slower still when it is not (Hassan et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The effect is substantial: Under typical viewing conditions, peripheral gratings appear approximately 10% slower at 6° and 20% slower at 32° eccentricity even when their perceived contrast is matched to that of foveal gratings, and slow gratings appear slower still when it is not <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hassan et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This underestimation is generally attributed to reduced spatial-frequency sensitivity, lower effective contrast, and noisier motion encoding at greater eccentricities (Blakemore & Snowden, 1999; Hassan et al., 2016; Mareschal et al., 2008; Orban et al., 1986; Thompson, 1982; Thompson et al., 2006).

text.text: A parallel asymmetry exists for perceived duration.

Peripheral stimuli are perceived as shorter in duration than foveal stimuli of the same physical duration, and the magnitude of this underestimation increases with eccentricity (Aedo-Jury & Pins, 2010; Bao et al., 2024; Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014).
text.formatted: Peripheral stimuli are perceived as shorter in duration than foveal stimuli of the same physical duration, and the magnitude of this underestimation increases with eccentricity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aedo-Jury & Pins, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bao et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The effect persists after cortical magnification scaling (Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014) and is not reduced by transient attentional cueing (Krug et al., 2024) or endogenous attentional cueing (Krug & Huckauf, 2025).
text.formatted: The effect persists after cortical magnification scaling <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014)</ref> and is not reduced by transient attentional cueing <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Krug et al., 2024)</ref> or endogenous attentional cueing <ref type="bibr">(Krug & Huckauf, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The direction of the effect may depend on the duration range: Krug et al. (2025) reported that while peripheral stimuli appear shorter at brief durations (20-220 ms), the effect reverses at longer durations (400-1,600 ms), possibly due to endogenous attentional shifts, and Upadhyayula et al. (2023) found longer perceived durations at 12° than at 3° eccentricity for durations of 750-1,525 ms.
text.formatted: The direction of the effect may depend on the duration range: <ref type="bibr">Krug et al. (2025)</ref> reported that while peripheral stimuli appear shorter at brief durations (20-220 ms), the effect reverses at longer durations (400-1,600 ms), possibly due to endogenous attentional shifts, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Upadhyayula et al. (2023)</ref> found longer perceived durations at 12° than at 3° eccentricity for durations of 750-1,525 ms.

text.text: However, these reversal findings, like the demonstrations of the underestimation itself (Aedo-Jury & Pins, 2010; Bao et al., 2024; Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014), were obtained with static or briefly flashed stimuli; whether continuously moving stimuli, which provide a sustained perceptual cue to duration encoding, produce the same pattern is unknown.
text.formatted: However, these reversal findings, like the demonstrations of the underestimation itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aedo-Jury & Pins, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bao et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014)</ref>, were obtained with static or briefly flashed stimuli; whether continuously moving stimuli, which provide a sustained perceptual cue to duration encoding, produce the same pattern is unknown.

text.text: The relationship between motion speed and perceived duration is also well documented and is perhaps the most robust finding in the time perception literature.

Faster-moving stimuli are generally perceived as lasting longer than slower or stationary stimuli of the same physical duration (Brown, 1995; Kaneko & Murakami, 2009; Karsilar et al., 2018; Tomassini et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Faster-moving stimuli are generally perceived as lasting longer than slower or stationary stimuli of the same physical duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brown, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kaneko & Murakami, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Karsilar et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Tomassini et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Whether the critical variable is speed per se (Kaneko & Murakami, 2009) or temporal frequency (Kanai et al., 2006; Linares & Gorea, 2015) remains debated, but the empirical pattern is robust: Increased motion speed lengthens perceived duration.
text.formatted: Whether the critical variable is speed per se <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kaneko & Murakami, 2009)</ref> or temporal frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kanai et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Linares & Gorea, 2015)</ref> remains debated, but the empirical pattern is robust: Increased motion speed lengthens perceived duration.

text.text: These three findings raise a natural question: Are the eccentricity-dependent duration underestimation and the eccentricity-dependent motion speed underestimation different manifestations of the same underlying mechanism?
If so, removing the speed asymmetry should also remove the duration asymmetry.

If, instead, eccentricity affects duration through additional, speed-independent mechanisms, such as differences in temporal integration, attention, or neural processing efficiency (Poggel et al., 2012; Tse et al., 2004; Zakay & Block, 1997), then a residual duration bias should persist even after perceived motion speed is equated.
text.formatted: If, instead, eccentricity affects duration through additional, speed-independent mechanisms, such as differences in temporal integration, attention, or neural processing efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Poggel et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Tse et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Zakay & Block, 1997)</ref>, then a residual duration bias should persist even after perceived motion speed is equated.

text.text: We refer to this eccentricity-dependent distortion of perceived duration as the foveal duration bias, adopting this term rather than the broader "eccentricity effect on perceived duration" used in prior work (e.g., Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014; Krug et al., 2024) to emphasize the directional pattern under investigation: a systematic bias toward judging the foveal stimulus as lasting longer in a direct comparison.
text.formatted: We refer to this eccentricity-dependent distortion of perceived duration as the foveal duration bias, adopting this term rather than the broader "eccentricity effect on perceived duration" used in prior work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kliegl & Huckauf, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Krug et al., 2024)</ref> to emphasize the directional pattern under investigation: a systematic bias toward judging the foveal stimulus as lasting longer in a direct comparison.

text.text: Crucially, none of the existing studies have isolated perceived motion speed as the mediating variable.
The present study was designed to fill this gap.
We tested these predictions using a two-phase within-subjects design.

In the calibration phase, each participant's peripheral motion speed underestimation (relative to a foveally presented stimulus) was individually measured at two eccentricities (near: 11.4°, far: 22.0°) using QUEST adaptive staircases (Watson & Pelli, 1983), yielding a point of subjective equality (PSE) for perceived motion speed.
text.formatted: In the calibration phase, each participant's peripheral motion speed underestimation (relative to a foveally presented stimulus) was individually measured at two eccentricities (near: 11.4°, far: 22.0°) using QUEST adaptive staircases <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Watson & Pelli, 1983)</ref>, yielding a point of subjective equality (PSE) for perceived motion speed.

text.text: In the main phase, participants compared the durations of a foveal and a peripheral random dot kinematogram (RDK) in a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) task under two speed conditions: physically equal (identical on-screen speeds) and perceptually equal (foveal speed unchanged, peripheral speed set to the participant's PSE; see Design below).
This design tests three predictions.
First, peripheral stimuli should be perceived as slower than foveal stimuli, with greater underestimation at the farther eccentricity (H1).
Second, under physical speed equality, a foveal duration bias should emerge: Peripheral stimuli should be perceived as lasting shorter than foveal stimuli (H2).
Third, equalizing perceived motion speed should reduce the foveal duration bias (H3).

If the eccentricity-dependent asymmetries for motion speed and duration reflect a common mechanism, equalization should eliminate the bias entirely; if a residual foveal duration bias persists, this would indicate that multiple, partly distinct eccentricity-dependent mechanisms are at play.

In sum, the present study provides a direct test of whether the eccentricity-dependent asymmetries in perceived motion speed and perceived duration reflect a shared mechanism (such that removing the speed asymmetry eliminates the duration asymmetry) or partly distinct processes that leave a residual bias even after speed is equalized. two eccentricities × two presentation orders × 16 durations, with random intercepts for participants; see below), assuming a random-intercept standard deviation of 0.25 on the logit scale, 256 equal-duration trials per participant, and a loss of 10% of trials to exclusions.
In each of 1,000 simulated data sets per sample size, the speed condition effect was tested with a paired t test on the participants' proportions of center-longer responses.

With a conservatively expected speed condition effect of OR = 0.90 (i.e., assuming a downward shift of P(center longer) by approximately 2.5 percentage points on the probability scale), power exceeded 80% at 55 participants, and reached 85% at 65 participants (α = .05).

This expected effect size was derived by reasoning from two independent literatures: Peripheral stimuli appear substantially slower than foveal stimuli moving at the same physical speed (Hassan et al., 2016; Johnston & Wright, 1986), and perceived duration increases approximately in proportion to log speed (Brown, 1995; Kaneko & Murakami, 2009).

text.text: Because these literatures use different paradigms and dependent measures (speed matching and duration reproduction/production, respectively), the expected OR for a 2IFC duration comparison could not be read directly from prior work; OR = 0.90 represents a deliberately conservative estimate of the predicted shift, chosen so that the design would not be underpowered if the true effect were small.
Our final sample of 66 participants meets the 65 needed for 85% power.
The foveal duration bias itself (H2) was well-powered (> 99%) at all sample sizes considered.

Stimuli were presented on an ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG27AQDM monitor (2,560 × 1,440 pixels, 0.229 mm per pixel; 120 Hz) using OpenSesame 4.1.8 (Mathôt et al., 2012) with the PsychoPy backend (Peirce, 2007) for stimulus presentation and PyGaze (Dalmaijer et al., 2014) for eye tracking.
text.formatted: Stimuli were presented on an ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG27AQDM monitor (2,560 × 1,440 pixels, 0.229 mm per pixel; 120 Hz) using OpenSesame 4.1.8 <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Mathôt et al., 2012)</ref> with the PsychoPy backend <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Peirce, 2007)</ref> for stimulus presentation and PyGaze <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dalmaijer et al., 2014)</ref> for eye tracking.

text.text: An EyeLink 1000 eye tracker (SR Research) recorded eye position at 1000 Hz throughout the experiment.
Participants sat in a dimly lit room, with their head stabilized by a chin rest, at a viewing distance of 57 cm from the screen.

At this distance, one pixel subtended approximately 1.4 arcmin at the center of the screen (43.4 pixels per degree); the visual angles reported below were computed from the pixel dimensions of the stimuli and the viewing distance.
The stimuli were RDKs displayed within circular apertures against a dark gray background (RGB: #3d3846; 12.6 cd/m²).
Each aperture had a diameter of 269 pixels, corresponding to 6.2° of visual angle at the screen center.
White dots (RGB: #ffffff; 279.3 cd/m²) with a diameter of 6.7 pixels (0.15°) were rendered at a density of approximately 8.2 dots/deg² (approximately 246 dots within an aperture).

All dots moved coherently (100% coherence, signal dots only) in a single vertical direction (upward or downward, each on half of the trials), with unlimited dot lifetime (i.e., no replotting of individual dots during a stimulus interval).
Dots were generated in a circular field six times the diameter of the aperture and were visible only inside the aperture, so that dots continuously entered and left the aperture.
A new set of dot positions was generated for every stimulus presentation.

The display contained five circular placeholders arranged horizontally: one at the center of the screen (fixation location) and one on each side at two eccentricities, 11.4° (near) and 22.0° (far) from fixation (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: The display contained five circular placeholders arranged horizontally: one at the center of the screen (fixation location) and one on each side at two eccentricities, 11.4° (near) and 22.0° (far) from fixation (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: These placeholders were drawn as thin (1-pixel) white outlines against the dark gray background and remained visible throughout each trial.
On each trial, the two active locations (center and one peripheral location) were indicated by thicker (4-pixel) outlines.
A small white fixation dot was drawn at each of the five locations.
The center stimulus always moved at 11.6°/s (502.7 pixels/s).
For the peripheral stimulus, speed depended on the experimental condition (see Design below).

The experiment used a within-subjects design with two sequential phases.
A QUEST adaptive staircase (Watson & Pelli, 1983) was used to estimate each participant's PSE for perceived speed between a foveal and a peripheral RDK.
text.formatted: A QUEST adaptive staircase <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Watson & Pelli, 1983</ref>) was used to estimate each participant's PSE for perceived speed between a foveal and a peripheral RDK.

text.text: Two interleaved staircases were run, one for each eccentricity level (near, far), with 40 trials per staircase (80 calibration trials total).
The staircase operated on a log₁₀ scale of the peripheral speed, starting at 10% above the center speed (12.7°/s), with a starting standard deviation of 0.15 log₁₀ units.
The target threshold was set to .50 (the 50% response point, corresponding to the PSE), the slope parameter (β) was 4.0, the lower asymptote (γ) was .01, and the lapse rate (δ) was .01.
The tested peripheral speed was bounded between 0.033 and 2 times the center speed (0.4 and 23.1°/s).
At the end of the calibration phase, each participant's PSE was extracted as the posterior mean of the QUEST distribution and converted to linear speed.
This participant-specific PSE was used to set the peripheral stimulus speed in the perceptually equal condition of the main phase.
Duration judgments were collected in a 2IFC paradigm.
On each trial, one stimulus appeared at the center of the screen and one at a peripheral location; participants judged which stimulus lasted longer.

On equal-duration trials, the design crossed four factors: speed condition (physically vs. perceptually equal), eccentricity of the peripheral stimulus (near: 11.4°, far: 22.0°), presentation order (center first vs. peripheral first), and stimulus duration (16 levels from 100 to 1,600 ms in 100-ms steps).
In the physically equal condition, the peripheral stimulus moved at the same on-screen speed as the central stimulus.

In the perceptually equal condition, the peripheral stimulus moved at the participant's individually calibrated PSE speed, such that the two stimuli were expected to be perceived as moving at the same speed.
On equal-duration trials (80% of all trials), both stimuli had the same duration.
On catch trials (20%), the center stimulus was 20% longer or 20% shorter than the peripheral stimulus, serving as a check on task compliance as well as making the task more engaging.

Each block contained eight catch trials with peripheral durations of 150 to 1,550 ms in 200-ms steps, alternating between a longer and a shorter center stimulus, each with a fixed presentation order and motion direction (upward on all longer-center and downward on all shorter-center catch trials).

The main phase was divided into eight blocks of 40 trials each (320 trials per participant), with each block fixing one combination of peripheral side (left or right of fixation), eccentricity, and speed condition.
Each block contained the 32 equal-duration trials (16 durations × 2 presentation orders) and the eight catch trials in random order.

Motion direction was fixed for each combination of duration and presentation order (upward for one order and downward for the other, alternating across durations), so that each direction occurred on half of the trials in each presentation order.
Block order was randomized.
Each session began with the participant reading and signing the informed consent form, followed by a brief verbal explanation of the task (~3-4 min).

Participants then completed a practice session (~5 min), which was a shortened version of the full experiment: It included a brief speed-judgment calibration block (10 trials at near eccentricity) and two abbreviated duration-judgment blocks (eight trials each, one per speed condition, with the peripheral stimulus on the right and durations of 200-800 ms), using the same response mappings and trial structure as the main experiment.
Following the practice session, the main experiment began with a standard 9-point eyetracking calibration.
Each trial within the session was initiated with a fixation-triggered drift correction (single-point recalibration) procedure.
Including consent, practice, and data collection, the full session lasted approximately 55-60 min.
Each calibration trial began with a drift correction, followed by the fixation display (placeholders and fixation dots; see Figure 1), which lasted approximately 461 ms.
text.formatted: Each calibration trial began with a drift correction, followed by the fixation display (placeholders and fixation dots; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>), which lasted approximately 461 ms.

text.text: The first stimulus (Stimulus 1) then appeared for 850 ms, followed by a blank interstimulus interval (ISI) of approximately 262 ms (SD = 13 ms), during which only placeholders and fixation dots were visible, and then the second stimulus (Stimulus 2) for 850 ms.
A jittered stimulus-response interval (SRI; 300-500 ms, uniform distribution) preceded the response prompt.

The fixed 850ms stimulus duration was chosen to ensure a long enough viewing period for stable speed percepts, and is also at the center of the array of durations tested in the main phase (see Main Phase Procedure below).
On each calibration trial, one stimulus appeared at the center and the other at the peripheral location; the order of center and peripheral stimulus was counterbalanced.
Participants indicated which stimulus appeared to move faster by pressing the "Up Arrow" key for center or either the "Left Arrow" or the "Right Arrow" key for the peripheral stimulus.
The response was scored as 1 (peripheral judged faster) or 0 (center judged faster), and the QUEST staircase was updated accordingly.

The trial structure was identical to the calibration phase (with the same ISI), except that Stimulus 1 and Stimulus 2 durations varied from trial to trial (100-1,600 ms, with catch-trial adjustments where applicable).
Participants now judged which stimulus lasted longer, responding with the same key mapping.
Responses could only be registered after the response prompt had appeared; key presses made earlier were discarded.
Brief breaks were offered between blocks.
Trials on which the participant's gaze deviated from the fixation location during stimulus presentation were flagged offline and excluded from analysis (see Data Processing and Exclusion Criteria).
Eye-tracking data were preprocessed using the Python eyelinkparser package (Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023).
text.formatted: Eye-tracking data were preprocessed using the Python eyelinkparser package <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Mathôt & Vilotijević, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A trial was flagged as a fixation loss if the average position of any fixation that ended during Stimulus 1 or Stimulus 2 (as detected by the EyeLink parser) was more than 135 pixels (3.1°, the radius of the central aperture) horizontally or vertically from the screen center.
Across all participants, 1,403 of 21,120 main-phase trials (6.6%) were excluded on this basis (per participant: M = 6.6%, SD = 11.6%, Mdn = 2.3%).

Fixation losses were concentrated in four participants, who lost 42.8%-55.9% of their trials; they retained 108-140 of their 256 equal-duration trials, whereas all other participants retained at least 206.

Trials with response times longer than the participant's mean + 3 SD (computed over all 320 main-phase trials of that participant) were also removed (357 of the 19,717 remaining trials, 1.8%; 1-10 trials per participant).
After all exclusions, 19,360 main-phase trials remained for analysis, of which 15,473 were equal-duration trials.
The dependent variable in the main phase (i.e., whether the center stimulus was judged as lasting longer) is a binary outcome on each trial.

We modeled these trial-level responses using GLMMs with a binomial family and logit link, which naturally accommodate unbalanced trial counts, binary outcomes, and between-participant variability via random effects (see Karsilar et al., 2025 Karsilar et al., , 2026)).

text.text: All GLMMs were estimated with the glmer function in the lme4 package (version 2.0-1; Bates et al., 2015) in R (version 4.5.2), using the bobyqa optimizer (maxfun = 100,000); convergence was checked with gradient and singularity diagnostics, and all models whose results we report converged without singular fits.

text.text: Stimulus duration (in seconds) was centered at 850 ms, the midpoint of the tested range.
Categorical predictors were effect coded (+1/-1), so that main effects and lower-order interactions are averaged over the levels of the other factors.

The preceding analyses establish that perceptual motion speed equalization reduces the foveal duration bias on average.
If this reduction is driven by the change in peripheral speed, then the equalization effect should scale with the magnitude of the speed correction applied.
To test this prediction, we fit the following exploratory model to equal-duration trials (Model 3):
Here, pse_ratio_c is the participant's eccentricity-specific PSE ratio (peripheral PSE speed / center speed), centered on the mean of all 132 PSE ratios (1.25, i.e., 14.4°/s).
A significant speed_cond × pse_ratio_c interaction would indicate a dose-response relationship.
The interaction was significant, Wald χ²(1) = 8.79, p = .003.

It was in the expected direction: Participants with larger PSE ratios (i.e., those who needed a greater speed increase to match their foveal percept) showed a correspondingly larger reduction in P(center longer) when that speed correction was applied.

The model-estimated equalization effect (OR, physically vs. perceptually equal) was 1.11 [1.00, 1.24] at a PSE ratio of 1.0 (11.6°/s), 1.24 [1.15, 1.34] at the mean ratio of 1.25 (14.4°/s), and 1.40 [1.26, 1.56] at a ratio of 1.5 (17.4°/s).

In the physically equal condition, in which all participants saw the same speeds, participants with larger PSE ratios showed a larger foveal duration bias (slope = 0.35 per unit of PSE ratio, 95% CI [0.04, 0.67], p = .029); in the perceptually equal condition, the bias showed no significant dependence on the PSE ratio (slope = -0.11 [-0.39, 0.17], p = .440).
Averaged over speed conditions, the PSE ratio main effect was not significant, Wald χ²(1) = 0.85, p = .357.
Model 3 fitted the data slightly better than Model 2 (ΔAIC = -5.8).

The interaction remained significant under all alternative exclusion criteria (all ps ≤ .006) and whichever participant was left out (all ps ≤ .017, random-intercept models; Supplementary Materials S7).
This dose-response relationship ties the reduction in foveal duration bias to the size of the individually applied speed correction (see Discussion).

In the present study, we tested whether the eccentricity-dependent asymmetries in perceived motion speed and perceived duration reflect a shared mechanism, by asking whether perceptually equalizing motion speed eliminates the foveal duration bias.

Using individually calibrated speed corrections derived from QUEST adaptive staircases, we found that equalizing the perceived speed of foveal and peripheral stimuli reduced the foveal duration bias by approximately 60%, but did not eliminate it.
In other words, the speed asymmetry, although substantial, accounted for only part of the duration asymmetry.
This suggests that eccentricitydependent asymmetries in perceived speed and duration reflect at least in part distinct mechanisms, because eliminating one does not fully eliminate the other.

The equalization effect also showed a dose-response relationship with the calibrated speed correction: Participants who exhibited greater peripheral motion speed underestimation showed a correspondingly larger reduction in foveal duration bias when that speed difference was removed.

Because a larger correction also meant a faster peripheral stimulus, one might ask whether the equalization effect is instead a generic consequence of increasing peripheral speed (e.g., through an arousal or salience mechanism).

Two further observations favor a link to perceived speed: Under physical speed equality, when all participants saw identical speeds, the foveal duration bias was larger in participants with greater speed underestimation, and after equalization the bias did not vary significantly with the size of the correction.

Our calibration measured each participant's PSE at 850 ms, the middle of the duration range, and applied it at all durations, which assumes that peripheral speed underestimation does not depend on stimulus duration.

The data are consistent with this assumption: The equalization effect did not vary with duration, either linearly or across the 16 durations, and it was in the same direction at every duration (see Supplementary Materials S4).
Because each PSE was estimated from 40 staircase trials, equalization cannot have been exact for every participant (Supplementary Materials S1).

Random error of this kind would not by itself produce a residual bias, and the absence of a relationship between the residual bias and the size of the correction (see above) argues against a systematic undercorrection proportional to the speed bias.

Finally, because the stimuli were shown on a flat screen, the peripheral stimuli were slightly slower and smaller in angular terms than their on-screen values imply; crucially, expressed in angular units, the calibration results and the dose-response relationship were the same (Supplementary Materials S6).
How do our findings relate to cortical magnification?

In a landmark study, Daniel and Whitteridge (1961; see also Talbot & Marshall, 1941) showed that, in primary visual cortex (V1), foveal vision is strongly overrepresented relative to peripheral vision.

text.text: This likely explains, at least in part, why many visual features, including motion speed and perceived duration, are underestimated in peripheral as compared to foveal vision.

However, the extent of foveal overrepresentation is relatively constant across different areas in the visual cortex, including area MT involved in motion perception, likely because all visual areas inherit this property from V1 (Harvey & Dumoulin, 2011; Tootell et al., 1995).

text.text: This means that differences in eccentricitydependent asymmetries between different visual features (such as motion speed and perceived duration) do not necessarily reflect differences in cortical magnification between the visual areas involved in processing these features.
Why, then, does removing the speed asymmetry leave part of the duration asymmetry in place?
A key observation is that the ability to distinguish between different motion speeds is relatively constant across the visual field (McKee & Nakayama, 1984).
text.formatted: A key observation is that the ability to distinguish between different motion speeds is relatively constant across the visual field <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(McKee & Nakayama, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Motion discrimination is a temporal task that requires integration of information across a large area, rather than a spatial task that requires high spatial resolution.
This likely explains why the eccentricity-dependent asymmetry for perceived motion is weaker than for most other features-though still clearly present.
But shouldn't the same apply to perceived duration?
Isn't time perception by definition a temporal task?
The counterintuitive answer may be that time perception is in fact not a temporal task in the same way that motion discrimination is.

Rather, as intrinsic (or distributed) models of time perception propose, perceived duration reflects aggregated activity across a wide range of brain areas, involved in processing a wide range of stimulus features (Ivry & Schlerf, 2008; Roseboom et al., 2019; Salet et al., 2022).

text.text: Many of the stimulus features that contribute to perceived duration are spatial and have a strong eccentricity-dependent asymmetry (Burr et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Many of the stimulus features that contribute to perceived duration are spatial and have a strong eccentricity-dependent asymmetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burr et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, perceived duration itself also has a strong eccentricity-dependent asymmetry, and equalizing only one of these features-perceived speed-would reduce, but not eliminate, the duration asymmetry, as we observed.
Taken together, our results are consistent with intrinsic models of time perception, at least when it comes to perceived duration of brief visual stimuli.
However, it should be noted that, because it is not known where in the brain perceived duration is computed, this argument is necessarily speculative.

In conclusion, the eccentricity-dependent asymmetries in perceived motion speed and perceived duration are partly but not entirely shared: Removing the speed asymmetry substantially reduced the foveal duration bias but did not eliminate it.
The residual bias after equalization suggests that eccentricity also influences temporal processing through mechanisms other than perceived speed.

Although the group-level results clearly confirm peripheral motion speed underestimation (H1; see main text), a subset of participants showed PSE ratios at or below 1.0 at one or both eccentricities, indicating no measurable speed underestimation in the calibration phase.

Specifically, 12 of 66 participants (18%) showed a PSE ratio ≤ 1.0 (a PSE at or below the center speed of 11.6°/s) at near eccentricity, five participants (8%) at far eccentricity, and four participants (6%) at both eccentricities.
These PSE ratios ranged from 0.62 to 0.98 (7.2-11.4°/s).
Several factors may explain individual PSE ratios at or below 1.0.

First, genuine individual differences in peripheral speed perception exist: Some individuals may show little or no speed underestimation at moderate eccentricities, particularly at near (11.4°) where the group-level effect is smaller.

Second, measurement noise in the QUEST staircase could produce PSE estimates at or below 1.0 even for participants who do underestimate peripheral speed on average; the staircase had 40 trials per eccentricity, which provides reasonable but not unlimited precision.
Third, the lower incidence at far eccentricity (8% vs. 18% at near) is consistent with the stronger group-level underestimation at greater eccentricities.
These participants were retained in all analyses.
Excluding them would bias the sample toward participants with the strongest calibration effects, potentially inflating both the H1 effect and the speed equalization effect (H3).
Their inclusion provides a more conservative test of our hypotheses.

text.text: A plausible explanation is that our RDK stimuli provide continuous coherent motion throughout the interval, supplying a sustained perceptual cue to duration encoding that does not depend on transient boundary detection and may override any transient-driven reversal.
Whether the discrepancy reflects a genuine stimulus-type difference remains to be tested.

In the main text, we report that perceptual speed equalization reduced the foveal duration bias from approximately 7.4 percentage points above chance to approximately 3.1 percentage points, accounting for 59% of the raw bias magnitude (95% BCa bootstrap CI: [41%, 78%]).

Because the GLMM uses a logit link, we verified this proportion on the logit scale to confirm it is not an artifact of the probability scale (logits computed from the unrounded means): logit(.574) = 0.300, logit(.531) = 0.123, logit(.50) = 0, yielding a reduction of (0.300 -0.123) /0.300 ≈ 59%.
This near-identity between the probability-scale and logit-scale estimates is expected when probabilities are close to .50, where the logit function is approximately linear.
The experiment script specified stimulus sizes, positions, and speeds in degrees of visual angle and converted them to pixels at a viewing distance of 57 cm.

Because the screen was flat, the angular size and speed of a stimulus also decreased with its distance from the screen center: At equal on-screen speed, the near and far peripheral stimuli moved 2.0% and 7.3% slower in angular terms than the central stimulus.

To validate the calibration procedure, we assessed the convergence of all 132 QUEST adaptive staircases (66 participants × 2 eccentricities).
Across staircases, the tested speed reversed direction 18.9 times on average (range: 4-28), and the responses alternated between "peripheral faster" and "center faster" 19.4 times (range: 7-28).

All 132 staircases met the convergence criterion of our analysis, a standard deviation of the speeds tested on the last 10 trials below 20% of the center speed: This standard deviation averaged 1.8% of the center speed (range: 0.7%-4.3%), confirming that the tested speeds had stabilized by the end of the staircase.
The mean QUEST posterior standard deviation was 0.027 log10 units (range: 0.023-0.036).

A cumulative Gaussian fitted to each staircase's 40 trials by maximum likelihood gave PSEs close to the QUEST estimates (median absolute difference 0.009 log10 units, about 2%; r = .84 on the log scale), with a median bootstrap standard error of 0.034 log10 units (about 8%).
Four participants lost fixation on more than 25% of calibration trials (overall 7.8%, per-participant Mdn = 2.5%); because fixation was assessed offline, these trials had updated the staircases.
All participants were retained in the main analyses; excluding the participants with high fixation loss did not change the conclusions (Supplementary Materials S7).
